eyebrow: Azure & AWS Cloud Security Engineering · Chapter 7
subtitle: Lesson 25 · Detecting and Responding to Cloud Attacks

steps.label: Committed to a public repo
steps.sub: Automated scanners find secrets in commits within minutes

steps.label: SSRF to instance metadata
steps.sub: Pre-IMDSv2, a web app flaw could leak an EC2 role's temp credentials

steps.label: Phishing or malware
steps.sub: Harvests a session, or reads ~/.aws/credentials straight off disk

code:
# the first calls after a leak are quiet and read-only
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name <leaked-user>
aws s3api list-buckets
aws ec2 describe-instances

# Azure equivalent
az account show
# Microsoft Graph: enumerate directory roles + app registrations
caption: None of this looks like an attack on its own — it looks like a script running describe commands.

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Look for a path to higher privilege — next lesson's topic

steps.label: Persist
steps.sub: Create a second, independent credential before anything risky

steps.label: Act
steps.sub: Only now: cryptomining, data theft, or lateral movement

code:
# MITRE ATT&CK Cloud matrix — this lesson's sequence, by technique ID
T1087      Account/Permission Discovery   (enumeration)
T1078.004  Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts  (the leaked credential itself)
T1098.001  Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
T1136.003  Create Account: Cloud Account   (persistence)
caption: Naming the stage by its real ATT&CK technique ID is how you write an incident report other analysts can trust.
